Building a Cyberdeck + TailsOS

Published on 2025-03-26 at 20:35 UTC+12 by Oscar N.
A collection of pictures featuring my Cyberdeck

Initial Idea

The ideal outcome of this project was to build my own cyber-deck using parts I had found around my room and to learn the best operating systems and services that provided the most anonymity and privacy. For those who aren't sure what a cyber-deck is, it is essentially just a DIY portable computer typically inspired by the cyberpunk genre (a science fiction subgenre set in a dystopian future. The cyberpunk genre pairs advanced technology, like A.I. and cybernetics, with societal decay and corporate control. I've seen a lot of people summarize the core idea as "high tech and low life" which is only becoming more and more truer and relevant as time going on).

This build some luck involved because the main keyboard I used perfectly fit into the top groove/outward top allowing it to be held in place while the components underneath it were untouched from the weight of the keyboard itself. The main brain of the computer was a Raspberry Pi 4B (4gb Memory) that my Grandad gave me. Powering this was a 20,000mah powerbank, connected to the Pi using a power switch very sketchily soldered onto the wires of a USB C cable. I'm not going to glorify the process of this, I basically just hacked away a little rectangle on the side of the case with a Swiss-army knife to slot the switch to. 

The screen I went for was a super generic 7.9 inch one from Temu, I'm not even sure on the brand to be honest. All of this was cased in my trusty tool box that I've had since I was about 8 or 9.

Operating System

One main OS I tried experimenting with on this Pi was TailsOS. Tails is an interesting OS because of the nature of how it runs. It's a security-focused, Debian-based Linux OS designed to protect your privacy and anonymity by routing all internet traffic through the Tor network, and if I understand it correctly, it loads the entire OS into your ram which means all the data is wiped when you shut down your device. I tried using Tails because the only real reason I saw myself using a cyber-deck compared to a much more convenient name-brand laptop would have to be due to privacy, and the research done seemed to indicate that Tails was the most "private" simply because it didn't save anything, each time you booted up the OS it was brand new. That also made it a bit annoying to use though for an everyday user.

Outcome

In the end my cyber-deck project was completed/ceased and I now have this little doomsday-toolbox sitting there ready to go. I think that in order to make the device way more practice in a 'doomsday' situation, you'd be best to download offline maps, the entirety of Wikipedia, and a mini LLM - all of which I ended up working out how to install on my phone rendering the cyber-deck project outdated for my personal life.
